gloss_terse: Chalchul, a town in the hill country of Judah near Hebron
gloss_readable: Chalchul was a settlement in the tribal allotment of Judah, mentioned in Joshua's geographical catalogue. Located in the hill country approximately four miles north of Hebron, this town has been identified with modern Halhul. The site preserves the ancient name through continuous inhabitation, a common pattern for place names in this region of Judah's highlands.

senses.1: A proper name for a specific town in Judah's inheritance. The multilingual evidence shows consistent transliteration (Chalchul, Jaljul, Chalchul) reflecting recognition of this as a geographic proper noun. Joshua 15:58 places it among the hill country settlements, and archaeological and geographical studies confirm the location near Hebron.

gloss_terse: to snatch, catch (a word from someone's lips)
gloss_readable: This rare verb describes the rapid seizing of something, particularly used metaphorically for catching words as they're spoken. In 1 Kings 20:33, Ben-hadad's servants eagerly seized upon Ahab's casual reference to 'my brother,' interpreting it as a sign of mercy. The image is of alert listeners who quickly grasp and act upon a favorable word before it can be retracted.

senses.1: To snatch or catch something quickly, especially words from someone's mouth. The context in 1 Kings shows diplomatic agents watching carefully for any sign of clemency. Spanish 'tomaron' (took/seized) and English 'caught' both capture the sudden, opportunistic action. The verb appears only once, making this a memorable snapshot of ancient Near Eastern diplomacy.

gloss_terse: Chali, a town in the tribal territory of Asher
gloss_readable: Chali was one of the settlements assigned to the tribe of Asher in the northern coastal region of Canaan. Listed in Joshua 19:25 among Asher's inheritance, its precise location remains unknown to modern scholarship. Like many minor settlements mentioned only once in boundary lists, this town's exact site has been lost to history, though it once marked a point in Asher's territorial description.

senses.1: A place name within Asher's allotment. The multilingual glosses (Chali, Halí, Chali) consistently treat this as a proper noun requiring transliteration rather than translation. Joshua 19:25 provides the sole biblical reference, situating it within the geographical framework of northern Israel's tribal territories.

gloss_readable: This feminine noun denotes personal adornment, specifically ornamental jewelry. Hosea 2:13 uses it alongside 'earring' to represent the finery that Israel adorned herself with while pursuing false lovers (the Baals). The prophet's imagery draws on the language of personal adornment to depict Israel's spiritual adultery—she decorated herself for idols rather than for her true husband, Yahweh.

senses.1: Personal ornaments or jewelry worn for adornment. The single occurrence pairs it with nose-ring or earring, suggesting items of feminine decoration. French 'bague' (ring) and Spanish 'joya' (jewel) reflect the ornamental nature. The prophetic context uses such luxury items symbolically to convey unfaithfulness and misplaced affection.

gloss_terse: and they shall profane it (with suffix)
gloss_readable: This Piel form with third masculine singular suffix means 'they shall profane it' or 'desecrate it.' Ezekiel 7:21 uses it to describe how foreigners will desecrate Israel's treasured sanctuary when God gives it into their hands as plunder. The verb conveys the deliberate defilement of what was previously holy, a recurring theme in prophetic descriptions of judgment.

senses.1: To profane or desecrate something holy, with the suffix referring to the sanctuary. Spanish provides both Kethiv and Qere readings, showing textual awareness. The multilingual evidence (profane, profanarán, profaner) consistently conveys defilement. Ezekiel's oracle uses this to depict the ultimate humiliation: the holy place given over to those who will treat it as common.

gloss_terse: Chelem (or Helem), a returned exile mentioned in Zechariah
gloss_readable: Chelem was one of the returned exiles in the post-exilic community during Zechariah's prophetic ministry. In Zechariah 6:14, he's mentioned in connection with the symbolic crowning oracle, though verse 10 refers to the same person as Heldai. Such name variations (Chelem/Heldai) were common in biblical texts. The name may derive from a root meaning 'strength.'

senses.1: A personal name of a man involved in the restoration community. Zechariah 6:14 identifies him as one of those who would receive a memorial crown in the temple. The multilingual glosses show transliteration patterns (Chelem, Helem, Hélem), treating this as a proper name. The textual variant with Heldai suggests fluidity in naming within the same narrative.

gloss_terse: purslain or similar plant with slimy juice
gloss_readable: This plant name appears only in Job 6:6, where Job asks rhetorically whether there is any taste in the juice or sap of this herb. The exact identification is disputed—suggestions include purslain, mallow, or the white of an egg (if the word is interpreted differently). Job uses it as a metaphor for something insipid and unpalatable, comparing his suffering to tasteless food that brings no pleasure or nourishment.

senses.1: A plant with bland, slimy juice used metaphorically for something without flavor or appeal. The Hebrew phrase asks about taste in the 'slime of purslain,' representing Job's complaint that his life has become as unpalatable as the most tasteless food. English 'mallow' and Spanish 'malva' suggest wild plants with mucilaginous properties. The image serves Job's larger argument about the meaninglessness of his suffering.

gloss_terse: Cheleph, a town in Naphtali's territory
gloss_readable: Cheleph was a boundary marker in the tribal allotment of Naphtali in northern Israel. Joshua 19:33 mentions it as one of the points defining Naphtali's territorial limits. Like many sites in these ancient boundary descriptions, its precise location has not been identified by modern archaeology. The name may relate to a root meaning 'exchange' or 'succession,' though the significance for this particular site remains uncertain.

senses.1: A place name marking part of Naphtali's boundary. The preposition 'from' indicates its role in geographical description—a starting or reference point in the tribal border. Multilingual versions (from-Cheleph, desde-Hélef, de-Cheleph) preserve the proper noun with appropriate prepositions. Joshua 19:33 provides the sole attestation in a list of boundary markers.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes the smooth, slippery quality of flattering or seductive speech. Proverbs 7:21 uses it to describe how the adulteress persuades the simple young man—with the smoothness of her lips she compels him. The word captures the polished, persuasive quality of speech designed to seduce rather than inform. It parallels 'abundance of her teaching,' showing how rhetoric can overwhelm resistance.

senses.1: The slippery, seductive quality of persuasive speech, particularly in the context of sexual temptation. The phrase 'smoothness of her lips' depicts speech that removes friction and moral resistance. Spanish 'suavidad' (smoothness) and French 'part' (though possibly a mistranslation here) engage with the slippery persuasiveness. Proverbs consistently warns against smooth-talking seducers whose words are more dangerous than obvious threats.

gloss_readable: This phrase refers to the smooth, rounded stones found in stream beds, polished by water action over time. Isaiah 57:6 uses it with biting irony: 'Among the smooth stones of the wadi is your portion'—meaning the Israelites worship common river rocks as if they were gods. The prophet's contempt is palpable: instead of claiming Yahweh as their inheritance, they've chosen worthless pebbles from a streambed.

senses.1: Smooth, polished stones from a brook or wadi, used here in prophetic condemnation of idolatry. The smoothness comes from water erosion, making these ordinary geological features. Isaiah's sarcasm targets those who treat natural objects as worthy of worship. The multilingual evidence shows both literal translation (smooth stones, piedras lisas) and some uncertainty, reflecting the interpretive challenge of this prophetic invective.

gloss_readable: This adjective describes smooth stones, specifically those David selected from a brook for his confrontation with Goliath. In 1 Samuel 17:40, David chose five smooth stones for his sling—stones worn smooth by water, making them aerodynamically ideal as projectiles. The detail adds realism to the narrative: David wasn't just grabbing random rocks but selecting the right ammunition for precision slinging.

senses.1: The quality of smoothness in stones, particularly those from a streambed. David's choice of smooth rather than jagged stones shows practical battlefield wisdom—smooth stones fly truer from a sling. The phrase 'smooth ones of stones' uses Hebrew's superlative construction, possibly meaning 'smoothest stones.' English and French preserve 'smooth' while Spanish focuses on 'stones,' both recognizing the tactical detail in David's preparation.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes flattering speech or smooth promises designed to deceive. Daniel 11:32 describes how a future tyrant will seduce covenant-breakers 'with flatteries'—using honeyed words to win compromisers to his cause. The plural form suggests repeated acts of flattery, a campaign of smooth talk. The word captures how autocrats often gain collaborators not by force but by making wickedness sound appealing.

senses.1: Flattering or smooth speech used to corrupt and seduce people away from covenant faithfulness. Daniel's apocalyptic vision shows flattery as a political weapon—the tool by which the wicked king gains Jewish apostates as allies. Spanish 'halagos' (flatteries) and French 'flatterie' precisely capture the manipulative sweetness. The context is prophetic warning about end-times deception through appealing lies.

gloss_readable: This noun refers to a subdivision or portion, specifically in 2 Chronicles 35:5 describing the divisions of Levitical father's houses. The context is Josiah's Passover, where the Levites are organized according to ancestral divisions to serve the assembled people. The term denotes organizational units within the larger tribal structure, ensuring orderly worship service during the major festival celebration.

senses.1: A division or subdivision within the Levitical organization, specifically of father's houses. The phrase 'division of the father's house of the Levites' shows nested organizational categories. Spanish 'división' and the contextual use all point to administrative groupings for temple service. 2 Chronicles 35:5 uses this organizational language to show the careful planning of Josiah's reformed Passover celebration.

gloss_readable: This is the gentilic form—'the Helekite'—referring to the clan descended from Helek. Numbers 26:30 uses it in the wilderness census, listing the Helekite family as one of the clans within the tribe of Manasseh. Like other gentilic forms in the census lists, it identifies descendants by their ancestral connection, turning a personal name into a collective clan designation.

senses.1: The collective designation for descendants of Helek, treated as a clan within Manasseh. The definite article makes it function as a group name: 'the Helekite family.' Multilingual versions (the Helekite, los helequitas, le Helekite) all preserve the gentilic pattern. Numbers 26:30 employs this in the systematic genealogical accounting that organized Israel's tribes during the wilderness period.

gloss_terse: Chelqai (or Helkai), a priest in Nehemiah's time
gloss_readable: Chelqai was a priest serving during the high priesthood of Joiakim, son of Jeshua, in the early post-exilic period. Nehemiah 12:15 lists him among the priestly heads of families in the restored Jerusalem community. The name may be an abbreviated form of Hilkiah, a common priestly name meaning 'my portion is Yahweh.' Such name variations and abbreviations were typical in genealogical records.

senses.1: A personal name of a post-exilic priest. The Septuagint rendering 'Chelkias' (similar to Hilkiah) supports the view that this is a shortened form. Multilingual versions show transliteration (Chelqai, Helcai) as expected for proper names. Nehemiah 12:15 places him in the genealogical framework of priestly families serving the Second Temple, part of the restoration community's reconstituted worship.

gloss_readable: This adjective, used substantively with the definite article, means 'the weak one.' Joel 3:10 uses it in a striking call to reverse normal expectations: 'Let the weak say, I am a mighty man.' The prophet envisions a day when ordinary distinctions of strength dissolve—even the frail will claim warrior status in the eschatological gathering. It's part of Joel's larger vision of cosmic upheaval and role reversal.

senses.1: A weak or feeble person, used substantively. The definite article ('the weak') makes it a class designation rather than a mere description. Spanish 'el débil' (the weak one) and French 'faible' (weak) capture the sense. Joel 3:10 uses this in prophetic hyperbole: when God acts, even inherent human weakness becomes irrelevant. The verse deliberately inverts the beatings-into-plowshares image elsewhere in prophetic literature.

gloss_readable: Hemdan was a descendant of Seir the Horite, one of the indigenous inhabitants of Edom before the Edomites displaced them. Genesis 36:26 lists him in the Table of Nations among Edomite clans. The parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 1:41 gives the name as Hamran, showing the kind of textual variation common in genealogical lists. Both forms appear to be valid representations of the same individual.

senses.1: A personal name within the Edomite genealogies. The Septuagint variations (Amada, Emeron, Amadam) show how different manuscript traditions handled the name. Spanish Jemdan and English Hemdan reflect standard transliteration patterns. Genesis 36:26 places him in the larger framework of Esau's descendants and the original Horite population, documenting the ethnic complexity of Edom's ancestry.

gloss_readable: Chammu'el was a member of the tribe of Simeon, listed in 1 Chronicles 4:26 in the genealogical records of Simeon's descendants. The meaning of the name is uncertain, though it may have Sabaean cognates suggesting possible Arabian connections. Like many names in the Chronicler's genealogies, it preserves the memory of clan leaders whose individual histories have been lost but whose names anchor family identity.

senses.1: A personal name within Simeon's genealogy. The name appears only in Chronicles' genealogical material, which often preserves names not found in earlier sources. Spanish Jamuel and the Septuagint Amouel show typical consonantal variations in transmission. 1 Chronicles 4:26 includes him in the Simeonite family tree, part of the Chronicler's effort to document all Israelite tribal lineages.

gloss_readable: This gentilic adjective designates the clan descended from Hamul, a son of Perez in the tribe of Judah. Numbers 26:21 uses it in the wilderness census to identify the Hamulite family as one of Judah's constituent clans. The definite article makes it function as a collective noun—'the Hamulite clan'—in the systematic enumeration of Israel's military-age males.

senses.1: The collective designation for descendants of Hamul within Judah. The gentilic pattern (personal name + ite) creates a clan identifier used in official census records. Multilingual versions (the Hamulite, los hamulitas, le Hamulite) preserve this as a proper group name. Numbers 26:21 employs it in the detailed tribal accounting that organized Israel's camp and military structure during the wilderness wanderings.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes someone who acts with violence or oppression. Isaiah 1:17 uses it in a command: 'Set right the ruthless' (or possibly 'Relieve the oppressed,' depending on whether it's active or passive). The context is Isaiah's call for justice in Jerusalem—genuine righteousness means actively intervening on behalf of those suffering under violent oppression. The rare word appears only here, making its precise nuance debated.

senses.1: One who acts ruthlessly or oppressively, or possibly one who is oppressed (if the form is passive). The Hebrew form suggests an active agent ('ruthless one') rather than a victim, but ancient versions varied. Spanish 'al opresor' (the oppressor) takes it actively. Isaiah 1:17's ethical imperatives focus on correcting social injustice, whether by restraining oppressors or defending the oppressed—both interpretations fit the prophetic call.

gloss_readable: This noun refers to curved lines or graceful curves, used in Song of Songs 7:1 to describe the curves of the beloved's thighs. It's part of the Song's celebration of physical beauty, using architectural or artistic language to praise the human form. The word captures the aesthetic appreciation of curved, flowing lines—whether in crafted objects or the human body's natural contours.

senses.1: Graceful curves or curved lines, specifically of the body. Song 7:1 uses it in the lover's descriptive praise, comparing his beloved's beauty to skilled craftsmanship. The plural 'curvings' suggests multiple flowing lines. Spanish 'las curvas' (the curves) and French 'les courbes' (the curves) precisely capture the aesthetic focus. The Song's use reflects ancient appreciation for symmetry and graceful form in human beauty.

gloss_readable: This word identifies a type of reptile listed among unclean creatures in Leviticus 11:30. It appears in a series of small creeping things—gecko, monitor lizard, wall lizard, skink, and chameleon. The exact species is uncertain; suggestions include sand lizard, chameleon, or other desert reptiles. Ancient Israel's dietary laws categorized such creatures as unclean, making them forbidden as food.

senses.1: A species of lizard or reptile deemed unclean under Levitical law. The context lists it among swarming creatures that crawl on the ground. Spanish 'caracol' (snail) shows the interpretive challenge—different traditions identified different creatures. English 'sand-lizard' reflects a common scholarly suggestion. Leviticus 11:30 includes it in the comprehensive list of prohibited animals, part of Israel's holiness code distinguishing clean from unclean.

gloss_terse: Chumtah (or Humtah), a town in Judah
gloss_readable: Chumtah was a settlement in the hill country of Judah, mentioned in Joshua 15:54 among the cities assigned to Judah's inheritance. Its exact location has not been identified by modern archaeology. Like many sites in these ancient territorial lists, the name survives only in the biblical text without clear connection to any known modern location. The Septuagint variations show how ancient scribes handled this relatively obscure place name.

senses.1: A place name within Judah's tribal allotment. Joshua 15:54 includes it in the geographical inventory of Judah's hill-country towns. The multilingual glosses (Chumtah, Humatá, Chumtah) show standard transliteration patterns for proper nouns. The Septuagint readings (Euma, Ammata) reflect different vocalization traditions, typical for minor sites whose pronunciation was uncertain even in antiquity.

gloss_readable: This adjective describes food that has been seasoned, particularly with salt or salty herbs, making it more palatable. Isaiah 30:24 uses it to describe the fodder that oxen and donkeys will eat in the messianic age—'well-seasoned provender.' The image suggests abundance and quality: even work animals will enjoy premium, flavorful feed. It's part of Isaiah's vision of agricultural prosperity in the restored creation.

senses.1: Food that has been seasoned to improve its taste, likely with salt or salt-herbs. The single occurrence describes animal fodder, suggesting that proper seasoning was valued even for livestock feed. Spanish 'sazonado' (seasoned) captures the culinary improvement. Isaiah 30:24's vision uses such details to paint a picture of comprehensive blessing—when God restores his people, even agricultural practices will reach optimal conditions.

gloss_readable: This adjective describes the red color of garments, specifically in Isaiah 63:1 where it depicts the Messianic warrior whose garments are red with the blood of judgment. The root may connect to blushing or turning red. The dramatic image presents God's chosen deliverer coming from Edom with crimson-stained clothing, having trampled the nations in the winepress of divine wrath.

senses.1: The red color of garments stained with blood. Isaiah 63:1 asks, 'Why are your garments red?'—answered by the image of treading the winepress in judgment. Spanish 'rojo' (red) and the contextual evidence all point to vivid crimson coloring. The prophetic vision uses this striking visual to depict God's victorious but violent judgment against the nations, comparable to grape juice staining a vintner's clothes.

gloss_readable: This participle describes someone who acts ruthlessly or violently. Psalm 71:4 uses it in parallel with 'wicked' and 'unjust,' asking God for deliverance 'from the hand of the ruthless one.' The word captures unrelenting, harsh treatment—someone who shows no mercy or compassion. It appears only here, making it a rare but vivid term for the kind of enemy the psalmist faces.

senses.1: A ruthless or violent person who acts without mercy. The parallel terms in Psalm 71:4 ('wicked,' 'unjust,' 'ruthless') build a picture of comprehensive moral failure—someone both legally unjust and personally cruel. Spanish 'violento' (violent) and English 'ruthless' both capture the harsh, unrelenting character. The psalm's cry for deliverance from such a person reflects the vulnerability of the righteous before brutal enemies.

gloss_readable: This Hiphil verb means 'and he repaired' or 'restored,' used in 2 Chronicles 33:16 of King Manasseh repairing the altar of Yahweh after his repentance. The context describes Manasseh's remarkable conversion—after years of apostasy and idolatry, he returns from Babylonian captivity, removes false gods, and restores proper worship. The verb captures the physical act of restoring the altar to functional condition for sacrifices.

senses.1: To repair, restore, or prepare (an altar or structure). The context in 2 Chronicles shows Manasseh actively reversing his previous religious policies—restoration of the altar signals renewed covenant commitment. Spanish 'restauró' (restored) and the French/German evidence all support reconditioning or repair. The verb emphasizes not just symbolic gesture but actual physical work to make the altar usable again for legitimate worship.

gloss_readable: This Qal verb with suffix means 'and she coated it' or 'smeared it,' specifically describing how Moses' mother waterproofed the papyrus basket. Exodus 2:3 tells how she plastered it with bitumen and pitch to make it watertight before placing her infant son in the Nile. The verb is denominative from 'asphalt,' turning the noun into an action—to cover something with asphalt or pitch as a sealant.

senses.1: To coat or smear something with asphalt or pitch as waterproofing. The single occurrence describes Moses' mother preparing the basket-boat for river exposure. Spanish 'la cubrió' (she covered it) and English 'coated it' show the application of protective material. Exodus 2:3's detail adds realism—the mother's desperate but practical action to protect her child, using the same waterproofing technique that made ancient boats seaworthy.

gloss_readable: This poetic word for wine appears in Deuteronomy 32:14, part of Moses' song describing God's provision for Israel. The phrase 'blood of the grape you shall drink as wine' uses elevated, archaic vocabulary fitting the Song's literary style. The term is borrowed from Aramaic, suggesting cross-linguistic influence in poetic diction. It denotes fermented grape wine, the standard beverage of celebration and abundance in ancient Israel.

senses.1: Wine, specifically used in poetic contexts with elevated register. Deuteronomy 32:14's Song of Moses employs this rare Aramaic loanword for stylistic effect, creating a formal, dignified tone. Spanish 'vino espumoso' (sparkling wine) adds a festive connotation. The parallel with 'blood of the grape' emphasizes wine's rich, life-giving redness. Poetic texts often drew on multiple language resources to achieve special effects.

gloss_readable: Chamran appears in 1 Chronicles 1:41 as a descendant of Seir the Horite in Edom's genealogy. He is the same person as Hemdan in the parallel list in Genesis 36:26, showing typical name variation between sources. The Chronicler's genealogical material often preserves alternative spellings or vocalizations of names found in earlier texts. Both forms represent legitimate renderings of the same ancestral figure in Edom's ethnic history.

senses.1: A personal name in the Edomite genealogies, equivalent to Hemdan in Genesis. The consonantal difference (Hamran vs Hemdan) reflects manuscript variation or dialectal pronunciation. 1 Chronicles 1:41 includes him in the Chronicler's comprehensive genealogical framework, documenting non-Israelite lineages relevant to biblical history. The Septuagint variations show how ancient translators handled these alternative name forms.

gloss_terse: and let him take a fifth part (as tax)
gloss_readable: This Piel verb means 'let him take a fifth' or 'collect a twenty-percent tax.' In Genesis 41:34, Joseph advises Pharaoh to appoint commissioners who will collect one-fifth of Egypt's produce during the seven years of plenty. The denominative verb comes from 'five,' making it mean 'to fifth'—to take the fifth part. This Egyptian taxation policy becomes the means of storing enough grain to survive the coming famine.

senses.1: To take a fifth part of something, specifically agricultural produce as a governmental tax or levy. Joseph's plan institutes a twenty-percent collection rate during abundant years for storage against famine. Spanish 'tome quinta parte' (take a fifth part) and French 'prendre un cinquième' (take a fifth) both capture the fractional taxation. Genesis 41:34's administrative detail shows ancient economic planning—state collection and redistribution preventing mass starvation.

gloss_terse: the fifth part (as tax or portion)
gloss_readable: This noun means 'fifth part' or 'one-fifth,' used in Genesis 47:26 describing the agricultural tax law Joseph established in Egypt. The text states that this fifth to Pharaoh became a permanent statute. However, the construction is grammatically awkward in the Masoretic Text, and ancient versions suggest reading 'the fifth' with the definite article, or possibly 'one-fifth' as a fractional designation.

senses.1: The fifth part of agricultural produce collected as tax. Genesis 47:26 codifies this as ongoing Egyptian law—one-fifth of the harvest belongs to Pharaoh, while farmers keep four-fifths. Spanish 'el quinto' (the fifth) and French 'le cinquième' (the fifth) treat it as a defined fraction. The verse describes how Joseph's emergency measures became permanent fiscal policy, an example of crisis-driven institutional change.

gloss_terse: Chammath (or Hammath), a fortified town in Naphtali
gloss_readable: Chammath was a fortified city in the territory of Naphtali, mentioned in Joshua 19:35 in the list of Naphtali's inheritance. The name means 'hot spring,' and it's likely the same as modern-day hot springs south of Tiberias, mentioned in Josephus and rabbinic literature. The site was known for its thermal springs, a notable geographic feature that gave the town its name and economic significance.

senses.1: A place name in Naphtali, probably identical with sites called Hammath-Dor and Hammon elsewhere. The name derives from 'hot spring,' indicating geothermal activity. Joshua 19:35 lists it among Naphtali's fortified cities. The multilingual glosses (Chammath, Hamat, Chammath) preserve transliteration. Ancient sources identify this with hot springs near Tiberias, making it a location known for therapeutic waters from antiquity through modern times.

gloss_terse: Chamath (or Hamath), father of the Rechabite house
gloss_readable: This Chamath (distinct from the Syrian city Hamath) was the father of the house of Rechab according to 1 Chronicles 2:55. The Rechabites were a nomadic or semi-nomadic group known for their strict vows, including abstaining from wine and refusing to build houses. Jeremiah 35 famously uses their covenant faithfulness as a rebuke to Judah's unfaithfulness. This genealogical note connects the Rechabites to Judah's family tree.

senses.1: A personal name identifying the ancestor of the Rechabite movement. 1 Chronicles 2:55 places him in Judah's genealogy, specifically connected to the families of scribes at Jabez. The preposition 'from Chamath' may indicate geographic origin or descent. The Chronicler includes this detail to show how the Rechabites, though distinctive in lifestyle, were integrated into Israel's tribal structure. Their ancestor's name is distinct from the northern Syrian city.

gloss_terse: Hammoth-dor, a Levitical city in Naphtali
gloss_readable: Hammoth-dor was a Levitical city assigned to the Gershonite Levites in the territory of Naphtali, mentioned in Joshua 21:32. The name combines 'Hammoth' (hot springs) with 'Dor' (perhaps 'dwelling'). It's likely identical to Hammath in Joshua 19:35 and Hammon in 1 Chronicles 6:76, showing how the same site could be referred to by variant names in different texts. The identification with hot springs near Tiberias remains probable.

senses.1: A place name for a Levitical city in Naphtali, probably the same location as Hammath/Hammon. The compound name may mean 'hot springs of Dor' or similar. Joshua 21:32 assigns it to Levites as one of their designated cities with pasturelands. Multilingual glosses show consistent transliteration (Hammoth-dor, Hamot-dor). The Septuagint variations reflect the challenge ancient translators faced with compound or variant place names.

gloss_terse: Chen (or Hen), a contemporary of Zerubbabel
gloss_readable: Chen was a figure in the early post-exilic community during Zechariah's prophetic ministry. Zechariah 6:14 mentions him in connection with the symbolic crowning oracle, where a memorial crown would be placed in the temple. The name means 'favor' or 'grace,' which has led some interpreters to take it not as a personal name but as a common noun. However, most modern versions treat it as a proper name alongside Josiah and Zephaniah.

senses.1: A personal name of a man in Zerubbabel's generation, though some interpret it as 'grace' or 'kindness' rather than a proper name. The context lists him with others who would receive memorial recognition in the temple. French 'et-grâce' (and grace) shows the interpretive alternative. Zechariah 6:14's oracle uses symbolic action to point to messianic fulfillment, and Chen (or 'grace') participates in this prophetic ceremony.

gloss_terse: the cells, vaulted chambers (in a prison)
gloss_readable: This noun denotes cells or vaulted chambers, specifically used in Jeremiah 37:16 to describe the dungeon where Jeremiah was imprisoned. The word implies rooms with arched or vaulted roofs, suggesting underground or semi-underground construction. The prophet was placed in these cells within 'the house of the pit'—a grim prison facility. The architectural term conveys the oppressive, enclosed nature of Jeremiah's imprisonment.

senses.1: Vaulted cells or chambers used as prison cells. The root suggests a curved or arched structure, possibly underground cisterns adapted for confinement. Jeremiah 37:16 describes these as part of a dungeon complex where the prophet suffered harsh imprisonment. Spanish 'las celdas' (the cells) captures the prison context. The parallel with 'house of the pit' suggests a multi-room underground facility designed for detention.

gloss_terse: to be gracious, show favor (infinitive form)
gloss_readable: This infinitive of the common verb 'to be gracious' or 'show favor' appears in Psalm 77:9 in a rhetorical question about God's character. The psalmist asks, 'Has God forgotten to be gracious?' The infinitive form emphasizes the action or capacity of showing grace as an essential divine attribute. The question itself expects a negative answer—surely God hasn't permanently ceased being gracious, despite current appearances of abandonment.

senses.1: The action of showing grace or favor, used infinitivally. Psalm 77:9's crisis of faith questions whether God has permanently set aside his gracious character. Spanish 'tener gracia' (to have grace) and the broader multilingual evidence show this is about God's fundamental disposition of favor toward his people. The psalm wrestles with how God's apparent absence squares with his covenantal commitment to be gracious.

gloss_readable: This plural noun refers to the embalming process, specifically used in Genesis 50:3 to describe 'the days of embalming' for Jacob. The text specifies this took forty days, following Egyptian mortuary practice. Egypt's sophisticated mummification procedures preserved bodies for the afterlife, and Jacob received this treatment due to Joseph's high position. The technical term captures the time-consuming process of preparing a body with spices and preservatives.

senses.1: The embalming process as practiced in Egypt, specifically the duration required for proper mummification. Genesis 50:3 notes that the standard embalming period was forty days, after which seventy days of mourning followed. Spanish 'los embalsamados' (the embalmed ones) takes it as substantive; English 'the embalming' treats it as the process. The detail shows how Joseph honored his father with full Egyptian burial customs while maintaining Israelite mourning traditions.

gloss_terse: his trained men (born in his household)
gloss_readable: This adjective describes trained, experienced, or tried men, specifically Abraham's 'trained men born in his house' in Genesis 14:14. These were 318 household retainers whom Abraham led in the night raid to rescue Lot. The term emphasizes they were not merely servants but disciplined fighters trained for combat—a private militia raised within Abraham's extensive household. Their birth in his house ensured loyalty and long-term training.

senses.1: Men who are trained, tried, and experienced, specifically household-born retainers prepared for military action. Genesis 14:14's detail shows Abraham commanded a substantial force of disciplined fighters—not hired mercenaries but men raised in his household and trained from youth. Spanish 'siervos de él' (his servants) understates the military implication. The number (318) and their household origin suggest a wealthy patriarch with a small army of loyal, capable warriors.
